title: By your grace
hook: the heading means by Your grace; ten verses follow

segments.voice: Yesterday, nitnem, the daily round, and your line, japji, then jaap. Today, the third morning bani begins.

Stand in line at a gurdwara near the end of the service and watch people's hands. A sevadar comes down the row with a bowl of warm karah prasad, the sweet made of flour, ghee and sugar. Nobody reaches in and takes a scoop. Each person holds out two cupped hands, and a spoonful is placed in them. Even a toddler learns it: hands together, open, waiting. You don't earn it at the counter. You receive it. The next bani of the Sikh morning has that same word written over its door.

segments.voice: Tav prasad. Tav means your; prasad means grace, a gift freely given. It's the same prasad as the sweet in your hands, and the same word that closes the Mool Mantar: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Guru Gobind Singh writes tav prasad as a heading again and again, over section after section, like a dedication at the top of every page. Here it heads ten short poems, the Tav Prasad Savaiye. A savaiya is a verse form of four long, swinging lines, made for reciting aloud. These ten come from the Tenth Guru's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless One, written in Braj, a literary language of north India in his day. Sikhs who keep Nitnem say them every morning, right after the Jaap, and they're among the five banis recited while the amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation. Here's the surprise. After a heading like by your grace, you'd expect soft, comforting verses. Instead the ten savaiye march past everything people in the Guru's world admired: ascetics and yogis, elephants hung with gold, emperors with beating drums, pilgrims at every river, rituals of every kind. After each parade, the verses set it all down and say, in effect, that without the Lord's love and grace it weighs nothing. So the heading is the key. Everything below it is what people try to achieve; the heading names what can only be received. Over the next week, the parade, one float at a time.
screen: `TAV PRASAD: BY YOUR GRACE.` · `THE SAME PRASAD AS THE SWEET.` · `TEN SAVAIYE, AFTER THE JAAP.` · `A PARADE OF WHAT PEOPLE ADMIRE.` · then, large: `BY YOUR GRACE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up and a little cupped, the way people hold them for karah prasad. Notice three things you're holding right now that you didn't make: the breath going in, the light in the room, the fact that you woke up today. If you pray, whisper Waheguru as each one lands.
Tav prasad, by your grace: the heading the Tenth Guru writes over these ten verses, from the same prasad as the gurdwara's sweet and the Japji's gur prasad.
Your line: cupped hands, waiting. Grace is received, never taken or earned. Until tomorrow, then.

original.note: Gurmukhi: by your grace. the heading Guru Gobind Singh writes over these ten verses and many of his others.

trapdoor: what you thought: tav prasad is just the name of a prayer.
what it means: by your grace. the heading says everything after it is received, not achieved.
what a scholar hears: tav is the old form of your, and prasad comes from a Sanskrit word for clearness, favor and grace, the same root as the sweet karah prasad.

chat.says: The savaiye have a heading, tav prasad. What does it mean?
options: By your grace: like karah prasad, it's received in open hands, not earned.
By your effort: the verses reward whoever works hardest at their prayers.
By your order: a command from the Guru to recite these ten verses daily.
chat.meaning: Tav means your and prasad means grace, a gift freely given, the same prasad as the sweet placed in cupped hands.

notes: Block B (Tav Prasad Savaiye, days 362–369) opens here; the teach previews the themes of the coming days without teaching their verses in detail.
Claim that Guru Gobind Singh writes 'tav prasad' as a heading over many sections of his compositions (Jaap Sahib, Akal Ustat and others): confirm wording.
Akal Ustat verses 21–30 as the Tav Prasad Savaiye: the commonly given numbering. Confirm.
Language described as Braj (Braj Bhasha). Confirm.
The five banis at amrit preparation (Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand) per the Sikh Rehat Maryada. Confirm.
Etymology: tav from Sanskrit tava (your); prasad from Sanskrit prasada (clearness, favor, grace). Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Karah prasad described as flour, butter (ghee) and sugar; received in cupped hands. Confirm.

Authorship: the script attributes the Tav Prasad Savaiye to Guru Gobind Singh, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada and Nitnem practice do. The authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth is debated among scholars, though the Nitnem banis are widely accepted. Keeper to confirm the plain attribution is appropriate.
